q: Which analgesic technique is usually used for open AAA repair?
why: GA with a thoracic epidural is standard; epidural analgesia continues after surgery.

q: During open AAA repair the aorta is clamped and BP rises to 190/100. What is appropriate?
why: Clamp hypertension increases afterload and myocardial ischaemia risk; treat by deepening anaesthesia or with a vasodilator (GTN).

q: How should clamp release be managed?
o: Optimise fluids, have vasopressors ready, and release slowly one limb at a time
why: Unclamping causes hypotension and acidosis; prepare with volume and vasopressors and release gradually.

q: What is the inheritance and gene defect in Marfan’s syndrome?
why: Autosomal dominant fibrillin-1 (chromosome 15): aortic root dilatation, dissection, lens dislocation, tall stature, joint hypermobility.

q: Which cardiovascular feature of Marfan’s syndrome is most relevant to anaesthesia?
o: Aortic root dilatation with risk of dissection
why: Aortic root dilatation, aortic regurgitation and dissection risk; avoid hypertension and tachycardia.

q: What is the normal anaerobic threshold on CPET?
why: An anaerobic threshold over 11 ml/kg/min is normal; lower values indicate higher peri-operative risk.

q: Which is an absolute contraindication to CPET?
why: Absolute contraindications include acute MI or unstable angina, uncontrolled arrhythmia, severe AS, acute myocarditis or endocarditis and uncontrolled heart failure or asthma.

q: Which scoring system predicts mortality specifically in AAA repair?
why: The Glasgow Aneurysm Score and Hardman Index predict mortality after AAA repair.

q: Which post-operative complication of AAA repair presents with bloody diarrhoea and a rising lactate?
why: Colonic ischaemia (often from inferior mesenteric artery loss) presents with bloody diarrhoea and acidosis.
